title: Advertisement of Multiple Paths in BGP
summary: This standards-track RFC defines a BGP extension for advertising multiple paths for the same prefix without the new ones replacing the old. Each path is identified by a Path Identifier in addition to the prefix.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally, when a router tells its neighbour about a destination, it can only mention one way to reach it. This document lets it mention several ways, each tagged with its own number, so that a second path does not wipe out the first.

questions: what is a bgp path identifier
subtitle: How BGP speakers can advertise several paths to the same prefix without each one replacing the last.

tldr.problem: Base BGP lets a speaker advertise only one path per prefix, because a new advertisement for the same NLRI implicitly replaces the old one.
tldr.mechanism: Each path gets a four-octet Path Identifier prepended to its NLRI, and peers agree to use it through the ADD-PATH capability, code 69.
tldr.outcome: Extra paths can help reduce or eliminate persistent route oscillations and give alternate or backup paths for better routing and faster convergence.

facts.label: Capability tuple
facts.value: AFI (2 octets), SAFI (1 octet), Send/Receive (1 octet)

today: RFC 7911 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2016, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The BGP specification defines an Update-Send Process to advertise the routes chosen by the Decision Process to other BGP speakers. No provisions are made to allow the advertisement of multiple paths for the same address prefix or Network Layer Reachability Information. In fact, a route with the same NLRI as a previously advertised route implicitly replaces the previous advertisement.

This document defines a BGP extension that allows the advertisement of multiple paths for the same address prefix without the new paths implicitly replacing any previous ones. The essence of the extension is that each path is identified by a Path Identifier in addition to the address prefix.

The availability of the additional paths can help reduce or eliminate persistent route oscillations. It can also help with optimal routing and routing convergence in a network by providing potential alternate or backup paths, respectively.
sections.plainLanguage: Two problems with the old rule. A router that advertises a second way to reach a destination makes the first one vanish, and that can set off a long argument between neighbours. And a router has no spare route to fall back on.

sections.title: How to Identify a Path
sections.content:
As defined in the BGP specification, a path refers to the information reported in the Path Attribute field of an UPDATE message. As the procedures specified there allow only the advertisement of one path for a particular address prefix, a path for an address prefix from a BGP peer can be keyed on the address prefix.

For a BGP speaker to advertise multiple paths for the same address prefix, a new identifier, termed the Path Identifier, needs to be introduced so that a particular path for an address prefix can be identified by the combination of the address prefix and the Path Identifier.

The assignment of the Path Identifier for a path by a BGP speaker is purely a local matter. However, the Path Identifier MUST be assigned in such a way that the BGP speaker is able to use the prefix and Path Identifier together to uniquely identify a path advertised to a neighbour. A BGP speaker that re-advertises a route MUST generate its own Path Identifier to be associated with the re-advertised route. A BGP speaker that receives a route should not assume that the identifier carries any particular semantics.
sections.plainLanguage: Each speaker numbers its own paths, and the numbers mean nothing to anyone else. When a route is passed on to another router, that router gives it a new number of its own.

sections.title: Extended NLRI Encodings
sections.content: To carry the Path Identifier in an UPDATE message, the NLRI encoding MUST be extended by prepending a Path Identifier field of four octets. The encoding specified in the BGP specification is therefore extended with the Path Identifier first, followed by the Length field of one octet and the Prefix field, whose length is variable.
sections.plainLanguage: Every route in an UPDATE message gets four extra bytes in front of it, holding the number that says which path this is.

sections.title: The ADD-PATH Capability
sections.content:
The ADD-PATH Capability is a BGP capability with Capability Code 69. The Capability Length field of this capability is variable. The Capability Value field consists of one or more tuples, each made of an Address Family Identifier of 2 octets, a Subsequent Address Family Identifier of 1 octet, and a Send/Receive field of 1 octet.

The Address Family Identifier is the same as the one used in the Multiprotocol Extensions specification, and so is the Subsequent Address Family Identifier. The Send/Receive field indicates whether the sender is able to receive multiple paths from its peer, value 1, able to send multiple paths to its peer, value 2, or both, value 3, for that address family and subsequent address family. If any other value is received, the capability SHOULD be treated as not understood and ignored.

A BGP speaker that wishes to indicate support for multiple address families MUST do so by including the information in a single instance of the ADD-PATH Capability.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending extra paths, the two routers tell each other what they can do: send them, receive them, or both. The announcement is a numbered capability, 69, and it says which kinds of address family it applies to.

sections.title: Operation
sections.content:
The Path Identifier can be used to advertise multiple paths for the same address prefix without subsequent advertisements replacing the previous ones. Apart from that, the route advertisement rules of the BGP specification are not changed. In particular, a new advertisement for a given address prefix and a given Path Identifier replaces a previous advertisement for the same address prefix and Path Identifier. If a BGP speaker receives a message to withdraw a prefix with a Path Identifier not seen before, it SHOULD silently ignore it.

For a BGP speaker to be able to send multiple paths to its peer, that speaker MUST advertise the ADD-PATH Capability with the Send/Receive field set to either 2 or 3, and MUST receive from its peer the ADD-PATH Capability with the Send/Receive field set to either 1 or 3, for the corresponding address family and subsequent address family.

A BGP speaker MUST follow the procedures defined in the BGP specification when generating an UPDATE message for a particular address family unless it advertises the ADD-PATH Capability to the peer indicating its ability to send multiple paths, and also receives the ADD-PATH Capability from the peer indicating its ability to receive multiple paths. In that case the speaker MUST generate a route update based on the combination of the address prefix and the Path Identifier, and use the extended NLRI encodings. The peer SHALL act accordingly in processing the UPDATE message.

A BGP speaker SHOULD include the best route when more than one path is advertised to a neighbour, unless it is a path received from that neighbour.

As the Path Identifiers are locally assigned, and may or may not be persistent across a control plane restart of a BGP speaker, an implementation SHOULD take special care so that the underlying forwarding plane of a receiving speaker is not affected during the graceful restart of a BGP session.
sections.plainLanguage: Withdrawing a path that was never announced is ignored, and the usual rules still apply to each numbered path on its own. When a router restarts, the path numbers may change, so care is needed that the forwarding still works.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
The extension provides a mechanism for a BGP speaker to advertise multiple paths over a BGP session, and care needs to be taken in its deployment to ensure consistent routing and forwarding in a network.

The only explicit indication that the extended encoding is in use in a particular BGP session is the exchange of Capabilities. If the exchange is successful, the BGP speakers will be able to process all BGP UPDATES properly. However, if a packet analyzer is used on the wire to examine an active BGP session, it may not be able to properly decode the BGP UPDATES because it lacks prior knowledge of the exchanged Capabilities.

When deployed as a provider edge router or a peering router that interacts with external neighbours, a BGP speaker usually advertises at most one path to the internal neighbours in a network. In the case where the speaker is configured to advertise multiple paths to the internal neighbours, and additional information is needed for the application, the speaker could use attributes such as the Edge_Discriminator attribute. The use of that kind of additional information is outside the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends have to agree, and only the agreement itself says so. A tool watching the wire cannot decode the routes unless it knows the exchange happened.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document defines a BGP extension that allows the advertisement of multiple paths for the same address prefix without the new paths implicitly replacing previous ones. As a result, multiple paths for a large number of prefixes may be received by a BGP speaker, potentially depleting memory resources or even causing network-wide instability, which can be considered a denial-of-service attack. This is not a new vulnerability, but one that is present in the base BGP specification.

The use of the ADD-PATH Capability is intended to address specific needs, for example eliminating route oscillations that were induced by the MULTI_EXIT_DISC attribute. While describing the applications for the ADD-PATH Capability is outside the scope of this document, users are encouraged to examine their behaviour and potential impact by studying the best practices described in the ADD-PATH guidelines document. Security concerns in the base operation of BGP also apply.
sections.plainLanguage: More paths mean more state to store, which an attacker could try to exhaust. The risk is already present in ordinary BGP and is not made much worse here.

fields.name: Path Identifier
fields.desc: Four octets identifying the path. Assigned locally by the advertising speaker.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: One octet, as in the base NLRI encoding.

fields.name: Prefix
fields.desc: The address prefix. Its length is variable; the figure shows it at IPv4 length.

viz.caption: THE SEND/RECEIVE VALUES IN THE ADD-PATH CAPABILITY (RFC 7911, SECTION 4)

items.label: Receive
items.desc: The sender is able to receive multiple paths from its peer.

items.label: Send
items.desc: The sender is able to send multiple paths to its peer.

items.label: Send and receive
items.desc: The sender is able to do both.

viz.caption: THE RULES THAT GOVERN THE EXTENSION (RFC 7911, SECTION 5)

items.title: Negotiate first
items.text: A speaker may send multiple paths only after it has advertised the capability with value 2 or 3 and received it from the peer with value 1 or 3.

items.title: Withdraw by number
items.text: A withdrawal for a prefix with a Path Identifier that has not been seen before should be silently ignored.

items.title: Best route included
items.text: A speaker should include the best route when it advertises more than one path to a neighbour, unless the path came from that neighbour.

items.title: Restart care
items.text: Path Identifiers may not survive a control plane restart, so implementations should take care that forwarding is not affected during a graceful restart.
